genZNote: The Enterobacterales you meet almost exclusively through a long-term urinary catheter — it thrives on catheter biofilms more than almost anything else in this family.

habitat.naturalHabitat: Human GI tract, soil, and water
habitat.hostAssociation: Can be part of normal gut microbiota in small numbers; strongly associated with long-term indwelling urinary catheters
habitat.environmentalOccurrence: Found in sewage and hospital environments, particularly long-term care facilities
habitat.reservoir: Human GI tract; long-term urinary catheters and long-term care facility environments

culture.colonyMorphology: Non-lactose-fermenting, translucent colonies; may swarm slightly on some media

identificationClues: Urease-positive, non-lactose-fermenting Gram-negative rod in the same biochemical family (Morganellaceae) as Proteus and Morganella
One of the most strongly associated organisms with long-term indwelling urinary catheters, particularly in long-term care facility residents
Intrinsically resistant to several antibiotics including polymyxins and tigecycline, narrowing empiric therapy options
Urease activity contributes to catheter encrustation and blockage, similar to the mechanism seen with Proteus

clinicalImportance.transmission: Nosocomial — associated overwhelmingly with long-term indwelling urinary catheters, particularly in long-term care settings
clinicalImportance.epidemiology: A hallmark organism of chronic catheter-associated bacteriuria in long-term care facility residents
clinicalImportance.labSignificance: Urease and phenylalanine deaminase positivity place it in the Proteus/Morganella/Providencia biochemical group; intrinsic resistance patterns matter for empiric therapy

examFacts.distinguishingFeature: The Enterobacterales species most strongly linked to long-term indwelling urinary catheters and long-term care facility residents
